GRIMMER-test many cases at once

Source: R/grimmer-map.R
grimmer_map.Rd

grimmer_map() applies grimmer() to every row of a data frame with means, standard deviations, and sample sizes.

Call audit() on the output for summary statistics. grim_plot_grid() accepts it as well.

Usage

grimmer_map(
  data,
  digits_x,
  digits_sd,
  x = NULL,
  sd = NULL,
  n = NULL,
  ...,
  items_averaged,
  data_type,
  sd_meaning = c("sd_sample", "sd_pop", "sd_sample_or_pop", "se"),
  rounding = "up_or_down",
  threshold = 5,
  symmetric = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

Data frame with columns x, sd, and n, and optionally items_averaged, data_type, digits_x, and digits_sd. Any other columns are returned alongside the results.

digits_x, digits_sd

Integer. The number of decimal places in x and sd, including trailing zeros. There are no defaults, since a numeric value does not keep them (1.40 is 1.4). Either a single number for the whole column or one number per row of data. If left out, they are taken from digits_x and digits_sd columns of data.

x, sd, n

Optionally, the names of the columns in data that contain these values, if they differ from the defaults.

...

These dots must be empty. Every argument after them must be named in full.

items_averaged, data_type

As in grim_map(), for x and sd.

rounding, threshold, symmetric, sd_meaning

Passed on to grimmer(), whose section Defaults explains the defaults.

Value

A tibble with these columns:

  • x, sd, n: the inputs.

  • items_averaged: the number of items averaged into each score.

  • data_type: the kind of data, as given.

  • digits_x, digits_sd: the numbers of decimal places, as given.

  • consistency: GRIMMER consistency of x, sd, n, and items_averaged. NA for a case that cannot be decided, such as one with a missing value.

  • reason: "Passed all" if consistent, or "Continuous data" if the test does not apply; otherwise the test that failed, or why the case cannot be decided.

  • Any other columns from data.

The reason column refers to GRIM and the GRIMMER tests of Allard (2018):

  1. The reconstructed sum of squared observations must be a whole number, and one that n whole numbers with the reconstructed sum can reach: at least the sum of squares of these numbers as close together as possible. For n < 5, some larger sums of squares are impossible, too.

  2. The reconstructed SD must match the reported one. Test 1 implies this, so it is never a reason.

  3. The parity of the reconstructed sum of squared observations must match that of the reconstructed sum of the values.

A negative sd gives "Negative SD".

Under sd_meaning = "sd_sample_or_pop", a consistent value set gives "Passed all (sample SD)" or, if it passes as a population SD only, "Passed all (population SD)". If the two conventions fail for different reasons, the reason names both, and audit() counts the sample SD's, as under the default sd_meaning.

The tibble has the class scrutiny_grimmer_map, which is recognized by audit() and grim_plot_grid().

Summaries with audit()

audit() on grimmer_map() output returns a tibble with one row and these columns:

  1. all_cases: total number of value sets.

  2. incon_cases: number of GRIMMER-inconsistent value sets.

  3. emp_incon: proportion of GRIMMER-inconsistent value sets.

  4. fail_grim: number of value sets that fail GRIM.

  5. fail_test1, fail_test3: number of value sets that fail GRIMMER's first or third test. Test 2 is implied by test 1, so it never fails.

References

Allard, A. (2018). Analytic-GRIMMER: a new way of testing the possibility of standard deviations. https://aurelienallard.netlify.app/post/anaytic-grimmer-possibility-standard-deviations/

Anaya, J. (2016). The GRIMMER test: A method for testing the validity of reported measures of variability. PeerJ Preprints. https://peerj.com/preprints/2400v1/

See also

explain_map() and explain_print() to explain each row's result in plain words.

Examples

# Use `grimmer_map()` on data like these:
pigs5
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>        x    sd     n
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1  7.22  5.3     38
#>  2  4.74  6.55    31
#>  3  5.23  2.55    35
#>  4  2.57  2.57    30
#>  5  6.77  2.18    33
#>  6  2.68  2.59    34
#>  7  7.01  6.68    35
#>  8  7.38  3.65    32
#>  9  3.14  5.32    33
#> 10  6.89  4.18    37
#> 11  5     2.18    31
#> 12  0.24  6.43    34

# The `consistency` column shows whether the values to its left are
# GRIMMER-consistent. If they aren't, the `reason` column gives the reason:
pigs5 |>
  grimmer_map(
    digits_x = 2,
    digits_sd = 2,
    items_averaged = 1,
    data_type = "integer"
  )
#> # A tibble: 12 × 9
#> # GRIMMER: default settings
#>        x    sd     n items_averaged data_type digits_x digits_sd consistency
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <int>          <int> <chr>        <int>     <int> <lgl>      
#>  1  7.22  5.3     38              1 integer          2         2 FALSE      
#>  2  4.74  6.55    31              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#>  3  5.23  2.55    35              1 integer          2         2 FALSE      
#>  4  2.57  2.57    30              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#>  5  6.77  2.18    33              1 integer          2         2 FALSE      
#>  6  2.68  2.59    34              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#>  7  7.01  6.68    35              1 integer          2         2 FALSE      
#>  8  7.38  3.65    32              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#>  9  3.14  5.32    33              1 integer          2         2 FALSE      
#> 10  6.89  4.18    37              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#> 11  5     2.18    31              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#> 12  0.24  6.43    34              1 integer          2         2 TRUE       
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: reason <chr>

# Get summaries with `audit()`:
pigs5 |>
  grimmer_map(
    digits_x = 2,
    digits_sd = 2,
    items_averaged = 1,
    data_type = "integer"
  ) |>
  audit()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   all_cases incon_cases emp_incon fail_grim fail_test1 fail_test3
#>       <int>       <int>     <dbl>     <int>      <int>      <int>
#> 1        12           5     0.417         4          0          1

# Explain the results in plain words:
pigs5 |>
  grimmer_map(
    digits_x = 2,
    digits_sd = 2,
    items_averaged = 1,
    data_type = "integer"
  ) |>
  explain_print(1:2)
#> GRIMMER test: x = 7.22, sd = 5.30, n = 38, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"
#> 
#> The mean was reported as 7.22, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming
#> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from
#> 7.215 to 7.225.
#> 
#> The mean of 38 integers is their sum divided by 38. So the sum must be from
#> 7.215 * 38 = 274.17 to 7.225 * 38 = 274.55.
#> 
#> A sum of integers is itself an integer, but there is no integer in this range.
#> The nearest ones are 274 and 275. They give 274 / 38 = 7.2105 and
#> 275 / 38 = 7.2368, which round to 7.21 and 7.24, not to 7.22. Since the mean
#> alone is impossible, the SD doesn't need to be checked.
#> 
#> ==> Inconsistent
#> 
#> GRIMMER test: x = 4.74, sd = 6.55, n = 31, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"
#> 
#> The mean was reported as 4.74, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding (assuming
#> either rounding up from 5 or down from 5), it could have been anything from
#> 4.735 to 4.745.
#> 
#> The mean of 31 integers is their sum divided by 31. So the sum must be from
#> 4.735 * 31 = 146.785 to 4.745 * 31 = 147.095.
#> 
#> A sum of integers is itself an integer, and 147 is in this range:
#> 147 / 31 = 4.7419, which rounds to 4.74.
#> 
#> The SD was reported as 6.55, with 2 decimal places. Before rounding, it could
#> have been anything from 6.545 to 6.555.
#> 
#> Together, the sum and the SD determine the sum of squares, which is what you
#> get by squaring each of the 31 values and adding them up. It is
#> (31 - 1) * SD^2 + sum^2 / 31. The values are integers, so their squares are
#> integers, too, and so is the sum of squares. What's more, an integer and its
#> square are either both odd or both even. So the sum of squares must be odd if
#> the sum is odd, and even if the sum is even.
#> 
#> With a sum of 147, the sum of squares is from
#> 30 * 6.545^2 + 147^2 / 31 = 1982.1753 to 30 * 6.555^2 + 147^2 / 31 = 1986.1053.
#> The integers from 1983 to 1986 are in this range, so one of them is odd, like
#> 147.
#> 
#> ==> Consistent
#>
